01.actor: The father of Shmuel and Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
01.event: A bill of divorce signed by one Androlinai of Neharde'a was found, and Shmuel's father sent the question of its validity to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia.
01.turn: No one knew whether the Androlinai named was the husband or another man of the same name.
01.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia replied that all of Neharde'a must be searched for another man of that name.
01.summary: A bill of divorce turned up in Neharde'a, written by a man named Androlinai divorcing his wife. Because it was unclear whether it was really her husband or someone else with the same name, Shmuel's father sent the question to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia in the Land of Israel. He answered that the whole city of Neharde'a should be checked for another Androlinai.

02.actor: Mar Zutra and a rebellious wife
02.event: A wife refused her husband, saying he disgusted her, and Mar Zutra compelled her to stay with him.
02.turn: Despite the coercion, the couple's union produced a great sage.
02.outcome: Rabbi Hanina of Sura was born to them, though the Gemara attributes this to heavenly help rather than a precedent.
02.summary: A woman rebelled against her husband, claiming she found him repulsive, and Mar Zutra forced her to remain married to him. From that couple came Rabbi Hanina of Sura. The Gemara adds that this good result came only through heavenly assistance and should not be taken as proof that such coercion is good.

03.event: A crooked alleyway in Neharde'a was required to have doors, by applying both Rav's and Shmuel's stringencies.
03.outcome: The alleyway was required to have doors.
03.summary: In Neharde'a there was an L-shaped alleyway, and the authorities required it to have doors, combining a stringency of Rav with one of Shmuel. The rest of the passage is legal analysis of why both stringencies apply.
03.missing: Who made the ruling and any consequence beyond the ruling itself.

04.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his weekly four dinars to a pauper through his wife, who came back saying the man did not need charity.
04.turn: She had overheard the household asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths, revealing he was wealthy.
04.outcome: Rabbi Hanina responded by citing Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers, since they excuse our failure to give enough to the truly poor.
04.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send four dinars to a poor man every Friday. One week his wife delivered it and returned saying the man did not need it: she had overheard his household asking whether he would dine on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina did not grow bitter; he quoted Rabbi Elazar that swindlers should be appreciated, because without them we would be guilty every day of neglecting the real poor.

05.event: Ulla, who often traveled to the Land of Israel, died outside it, and Rabbi Elazar was told.
05.turn: Rabbi Elazar lamented that Ulla died in an unclean land; told that his coffin was being brought to Israel, he was not consoled.
05.outcome: Rabbi Elazar said that being received by the land in life is not like being received after death.
05.summary: Ulla regularly went up to the Land of Israel, but he died abroad. When Rabbi Elazar heard, he mourned him with the verse about dying in an unclean land. People told him Ulla's coffin was coming for burial in Israel, but he replied that being absorbed by the land after death is not the same as being absorbed while alive.

07.actor: A dying man, his heirs and his daughter
07.event: A man bequeathed a palm tree to his daughter but left only two half-shares of palm trees.
07.turn: The heirs wanted to give her the two halves, raising the question of whether two halves count as a palm tree.
07.outcome: Rav Mordekhai cited Rava that people do call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs could give her the halves.
07.summary: A man's will left a palm tree to his daughter, but when he died the estate held only two half-shares of palm trees owned with partners. The heirs wanted to give her those two halves. Rav Ashi wondered whether that fulfilled the father's words, and Rav Mordekhai reported in Rava's name that people do speak of two halves as a palm tree, so the heirs' offer stood.

08.event: Rabbi ruled in a case according to Rabbi Elazar's opinion.
08.turn: He afterwards remembered something about that ruling.
08.outcome: He said Rabbi Elazar is worthy of reliance in exigent circumstances.
08.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once ruled in accordance with Rabbi Elazar. Afterward he recalled that his ruling was questionable, and said that Rabbi Elazar is a worthy authority to rely on in a time of pressing need.
08.missing: The details of the case he ruled on, and what exactly he remembered.

09.event: Mar Yehuda found the residents of Mavrakhta placing their eiruv in a synagogue and told them to put it farther in to gain more distance.
09.turn: Rava rebuked him, calling him argumentative.
09.outcome: Rava declared that no one follows Rabbi Akiva's view on this in eiruv law, so the placement made no difference.
09.summary: Mar Yehuda came upon the people of Mavrakhta placing their eiruv in the synagogue of Beit Agovar and advised them to set it farther inside so they could walk farther on Shabbat. Rava scolded him as a contrarian, saying that in eiruv matters nobody follows the opinion of Rabbi Akiva that his advice relied on.

10.actor: Rava and one of the Sages
10.event: Rava boasted that he was like ben Azzai in the markets of Tiberias, ready for any question.
10.turn: A Sage asked how many apples are needed for an eiruv; Rava answered that apples cannot be used, and the Sage challenged him from a mishna.
10.summary: In high spirits, Rava declared himself as sharp as ben Azzai and ready to answer anything. A scholar promptly asked him how many apples are needed for an eiruv. Rava retorted that apples are not used for an eiruv, but the scholar cited a mishna implying that all foods combine for an eiruv.
10.missing: How the exchange ends, i.e., Rava's response to the challenge.

11.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
11.event: They bought a maidservant for copper coins but, lacking the money, left a piece of silver as collateral.
11.turn: The price of the maidservant rose and the sellers wanted to back out.
11.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled that neither coins nor collateral had effected the sale, so it was void.
11.summary: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin agreed to buy a maidservant for copper coins, but since they did not have the coins they deposited a piece of silver as security. When her price went up, the sellers wanted to cancel. Rabbi Ami ruled that no payment and no valid collateral had changed hands, so there was no sale.

12.event: Seven teachings said on Shabbat morning before Rav Hisda in Sura were repeated before Rava in Pumbedita at the end of that Shabbat.
12.turn: The distance was too great to travel on Shabbat, raising who carried them.
12.summary: Seven teachings were said one Shabbat morning before Rav Hisda in Sura and were heard again before Rava in Pumbedita late that same Shabbat, though the distance could not be walked on Shabbat. The passage cites this only as evidence; who brought them is debated afterwards as a legal point.
12.missing: Who carried the teachings and how; the passage only gestures at the incident.

13.actor: Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zerika
13.event: Rabbi Ami was asked whether a master may take payment for a slave who ran off to a foreign army; Rabbi Yirmeya sent Rabbi Zerika to search the sources.
13.turn: Rabbi Zerika found a baraita about a house seized by a gentile that supplied an answer.
13.outcome: Rabbi Ami sent out a ruling to all Israel that the master may take the slave's value and register it in gentile courts.
13.summary: Rabbi Ami was asked about a slave who fled and joined a foreign army beyond his master's reach: could the master accept the slave's price? Rabbi Yirmeya told Rabbi Zerika to check his sources, and he found a teaching permitting a Jew to take payment for a house a gentile seized by force. Rabbi Ami then issued a public ruling that the master may take the slave's value, since he is like one rescuing money from their hands.
13.missing: The passage is mainly a legal inquiry; there is little narrative beyond the question, search and ruling.

14.actor: A man who gave a conditional divorce
14.event: A man said his bill of divorce would take effect if he did not return within thirty days, and he came back just at the end.
14.turn: The ferry was on the far side of the river, so he could not cross in time and shouted, 'See that I have come.'
14.outcome: Shmuel ruled that this did not count as returning.
14.summary: A man gave agents a bill of divorce, saying it should take effect if he had not returned within thirty days. He arrived at the river at the last moment but the ferry was on the other side, and he could only call across, 'See, I have come!' Shmuel ruled that this was not a return, so the condition was fulfilled.

15.event: Rava asked Rav Nahman which tanna rejects retroactive designation even for rabbinic laws, citing a baraita.
15.turn: Rav Nahman was silent and gave no answer.
15.outcome: Rav Nahman said nothing, since he did not accept the version of the school of Ayo that could have answered.
15.summary: Rava challenged Rav Nahman to identify the tanna behind a teaching that rejects retroactive designation even in rabbinic matters. Rav Nahman fell silent and said nothing at all. The Gemara explains he could have cited the school of Ayo but did not accept that tradition.
15.missing: This is mostly a scholarly exchange; the only event is the question and the silence.

16.event: Rav Dimi was stumped by a challenge, and Abaye suggested the answer from a verse.
16.turn: Abaye's answer matched Rabbi Yohanan's own teaching.
16.outcome: Rav Dimi praised Abaye as though he had been present when Rabbi Yohanan taught it.
16.summary: Rav Dimi, faced with a difficulty about a teaching of Rabbi Yohanan, fell silent. Abaye proposed that the case was different because the verse ties the matter to birth. Rav Dimi praised him, saying he had seen Abaye's head among the pillars when Rabbi Yohanan taught it, meaning Abaye understood it as if he had been there.
16.missing: The start of the exchange (the challenge Rav Dimi faced) is only partly reconstructed from the preceding legal argument.

17.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
17.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba met Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying a child to the synagogue to study with only a cheap covering on his head.
17.turn: Asked why the haste, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cited the verse linking teaching one's children with standing at Sinai.
17.outcome: From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat breakfast before teaching his child.
17.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing a child to the synagogue to learn, a cheap cloth thrown over his head. When asked what the hurry was, he answered that Scripture places teaching one's descendants right next to standing before God at Sinai. Taking this to heart, Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba never again ate breakfast until he had reviewed and advanced his child's lessons.

18.event: An incident occurred in Rav Hisda's study hall and was brought to Rav Huna's study hall.
18.outcome: They resolved it from a mishna about an agent and consecrated property.
18.summary: Some case arose in Rav Hisda's study hall, and Rav Hisda took it to Rav Huna's study hall, where it was decided on the basis of a mishna about unspoken intentions. The rest is legal reasoning.
18.missing: What the incident actually was; the passage only mentions that one happened.

19.actor: A blind man who studied with Mar Shmuel
19.event: The blind man was late, Mar Shmuel sent a messenger who missed him on the road, and the messenger reported that he saw the man's wife committing adultery.
19.turn: On a single witness's word, the blind man had to decide whether to divorce his wife.
19.outcome: Mar Shmuel told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not otherwise.
19.summary: A blind man used to recite mishnayot before Mar Shmuel. One day he was late, so Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to fetch him; they took different routes and missed each other, and the messenger ended up at the blind man's house. He returned claiming he had seen the man's wife commit adultery. Mar Shmuel told the blind man to divorce her if he believed the messenger, and otherwise not to.

20.event: Rabbi Akiva picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and separated two tithes from it.
20.turn: He tithed it according to both Beit Shammai's and Beit Hillel's new-year dates.
20.summary: Rabbi Akiva once picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and separated from it two different tithes, one according to Beit Shammai, who count that day as the new year for trees, and one according to Beit Hillel, who count the fifteenth. It is a single act cited as evidence, without a real turn or consequence.
20.missing: Any consequence of his act; it is a brief precedent rather than a full story.
